chain: Smoking and drinking irritate vocal cords
whisky-and-cigar-voice-fad.text: Some online circles promote smoking and drinking as a way to get a deep, husky voice that sounds attractive. The voice change itself is documented in some smokers, but as a sign of vocal cord disease; its attractiveness benefit rests on anecdote.

deep-voice-masculinity-meta.text: Looksmaxxing forums hold that a deeper voice signals masculinity and dominance and so raises perceived attractiveness and status. Voice physiology is well described, while the social-perception claim is discussed mostly through anecdote in these circles.

voice-transformation-software.text: Voice changers alter pitch or timbre in real time or in post-processing, so a speaker can sound deeper or more resonant in calls, streams and recordings. The change is audible immediately; its use for appearance is mostly discussed informally and has not been studied.

podcast-mic-and-eq-boost.text: Users pair a close, directional microphone with a low-frequency EQ boost so recordings sound deeper, fuller and more resonant. The effect is audible straight away on recordings, though the speaker's own voice stays the same.

accent-training.text: People take accent coaching to be understood more easily or to sound closer to a target accent, which feeds into how polished they come across. Linguists note it takes sustained practice, and its effect on perceived appearance has not been studied.

speech-pacing-apps.text: Users practice speaking speed and pauses with apps because listeners form impressions of confidence from pace. Pace and impressions are researched in general, while the apps themselves have not been tested for appearance outcomes.

chain: Repeated practice in front of audiences
public-speaking-course.text: People take public speaking courses to build confidence and delivery, which they see as part of coming across as more commanding. Confidence gains are reported for such training, but little direct trial evidence addresses appearance-related outcomes.

ear-training.text: Borrowed from music education, ear training is mentioned in voice discussions as a way to become aware of and control vocal pitch. It is well established for music skills, while its use for voice appearance is anecdotal and unstudied.

tongue-stretching-exercises.text: Forum posters say tongue stretches lower the voice. The only trial found involves swallowing rehabilitation after stroke, so the voice-deepening idea rests on anecdote.

gym-and-loud-lifting-for-voice.text: A folk belief in voice-focused corners of appearance culture holds that weight training, especially grunting or shouting while lifting, deepens the voice. No published study located has tested it.

chain: Drier clothes, less odor, fresher presence
antiperspirant.text: Antiperspirants reduce underarm sweat with aluminium salts, keeping shirts dry and cutting the moisture odor-causing bacteria feed on. It is the everyday hygiene staple in grooming routines, and sweat reduction is measurable.

deodorant.text: Deodorants are applied to the underarms to control body odor, the basic scent-hygiene step in grooming, on the premise that smell affects perceived attractiveness. Odor control is immediately noticeable, though claims like skipping soap for an ideal scent are anecdotal.

clinical-strength-antiperspirant.text: Heavy sweaters use these stronger over-the-counter antiperspirants as a step before prescription options, to keep clothing dry and underarms fresh. Topical antiperspirants are listed as first-line care for hyperhidrosis in guidelines.

chain: Strong aluminium chloride blocks sweat ducts
aluminum-chloride-prescription-drysol.text: Prescription aluminium chloride is used for heavy sweating, to stay dry and avoid visible sweat marks and odor. Guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line therapy, and the product is established for hyperhidrosis.

botox-for-underarm-sweat.text: Clinic-delivered botulinum toxin injections switch off underarm sweat glands for months, appealing to people who want dry clothes and less odor. It is studied for axillary hyperhidrosis, with limited research on its use for odor specifically.

miradry.text: miraDry is a clinic microwave treatment aimed at long-lasting reduction of underarm sweat and odor. It is FDA-cleared for axillary hyperhidrosis and studied in several trials, and its odor use is a secondary indication.

axillary-sweat-gland-suction.text: This minor surgery removes or disrupts underarm sweat glands for people seeking lasting dryness and less odor. Evidence in our sources comes from small registered trials.

glycopyrronium-wipes-qbrexza.text: Prescription glycopyrronium wipes are applied to the underarms to cut excessive sweating and keep clothes dry. The FDA approved topical glycopyrronium for primary axillary hyperhidrosis in 2018, so the sweat effect is studied.

chain: Dry skin and clothes, less odor
oxybutynin-for-sweating.text: Oxybutynin is a bladder drug used off-label to reduce excessive sweating, so users can stay dry and avoid sweat marks. A placebo-controlled trial supports the sweat reduction; the appearance benefit is a side use of the drug.

chain: Sweat glands in palms and soles quieted
iontophoresis.text: Iontophoresis uses a low electric current to treat sweaty palms and soles, helping people keep hands dry and feet less odorous. It has been used since the 1950s for hyperhidrosis, and its role in appearance is mainly dryness.

chain: Less surface for sweat and bacteria
armpit-shaving.text: Shaving the underarms gives a smooth, groomed look at once and is proposed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to cut odor held by hair. The one study found shaved and unshaved armpits smelled the same.

pit-hair-laser-removal.text: Laser hair removal gives lasting smooth underarms, and is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a lasting way to reduce armpit odor by removing hair. The hair reduction is visible; the odor benefit is untested.

chain: Acid exfoliates and lowers skin pH
acid-body-wash-aha-bha-for-pits.text: Users apply AHA or BHA washes to the armpits on the theory that lower pH and removal of dead skin starves odor bacteria. The idea is plausible chemically but untested for odor.

benzoyl-peroxide-wash-for-body-odor.text: An acne wash repurposed for armpits and body, used on the theory that it kills odor-producing bacteria. Its antibacterial role in acne is established, while its use for odor is untested.

antibacterial-soap-hibiclens.text: Hibiclens, a hospital chlorhexidine antiseptic wash, is used by looksmaxxing posters on underarms to reduce odor-causing bacteria. Its antibacterial action is established; odor outcomes have not been tested.

zinc-based-deodorant-zinc-ricinoleate.text: Zinc ricinoleate, a castor-oil zinc salt, is added to deodorants as an odor-adsorbing ingredient and mentioned as an alternative to aluminium antiperspirants. The mechanism is unclear and no trials were found.

mandelic-acid-deodorant-lume.text: Mandelic acid deodorants, best known through Lume, use an acid-based formula instead of aluminium to control odor. The chemistry is plausible, but no deodorant trials exist.

lume-whole-body-deodorant.text: Lume is a viral acid-based deodorant sold for the whole body, discussed on short-video platforms as a non-aluminium option. Its popularity is clear; it has not been tested in trials.

magnesium-deodorant.text: Magnesium hydroxide deodorants, including milk of magnesia, are used as natural aluminium-free options for underarm odor. They are popular, but no trials were found.

chain: Alum salt rubbed on damp skin
crystal-deodorant-alum-stone.text: Alum stones are rubbed on skin as a natural, fragrance-free deodorant with ancient use. Published evidence is limited to irritation case reports, so odor control rests on tradition and anecdote.
